title: The future withسَـ‎ e ‎سَوْفَ‎ · ‎لَنْand the conjunctive

blocks.text: In this unit you learn to talk about projects: what you will do, what you will not do, what you want, must and can do. The future is simple, just a prefix; the real grammatical novelty is the conjunctiva ( ⁧المَنْصُوب⁩ ), the manner of the verb that follows ⁧أَنْ⁩ . ⁧لَنْ⁩ Not (in the future) and particles of purpose. In Arabic, the conjunctive expresses no doubt, as in English: it is an obligatory form after certain words. From here also the story of this level: Salmā invites Luke and Mary to Cairo for the summer. Two weeks.

What to notice. ⁧سَتَفْعَلُ⁩ , ⁧سَأَبْقَى⁩ , ⁧سَنَزُورُ⁩ : the future is the imperfect with ⁧سَـ⁩ Attacked. ⁧بَعْدُ⁩ (a) u) after a denial it means "still": ⁧لَا أَعْرِفُ بَعْدُ⁩ I don't know yet. The future is formed by putting ⁧سَـ⁩ (a) or ⁧سَوْفَ⁩ (sawfa) in front of the imperfect indicative . The verb doesn't change.
⁧سَوْفَ يَدْعُونَسَيَدْعُونَيَدْعُونَ⁩ invite

Difference in use. The meaning is the same. ⁧سَـ⁩ is more frequent and neutral; ⁧سَوْفَ⁩ is more formal, hears itself in speeches and often indicates a future farther or more decisive. In newspaper headlines, you often find only the imperfect (A2-03) with value of near future. Spelling. ⁧سَـ⁩ writes attached to the verb and leaves no room: ⁧سَأَكْتُبُ⁩ , not * ⁧سَ أَكْتُبُ⁩ . ⁧سَوْفَ⁩ It's a separate word. Neither one attaches itself to other parts of the speech: the future is not used with nominal phrases, which have no verb. The future of ⁧كَانَ⁩ : ⁧سَيَكُونُ الاِجْتِمَاعُ طَوِيلًا⁩ The meeting will be long, with the predicate to the accusative as after ⁧كَانَ⁩ ( A1-18). ⁧إِنْ شَاءَ اللهُ⁩ . In Arabic use, a future project is often accompanied by this formula, even among non-religious people: ⁧سَأَرَاكَ غَدًا، إِنْ شَاءَ اللهُ⁩ See you tomorrow, if God wills. It's courtesy, not uncertainty; But beware of the tone: in certain contexts it can also be a kind way not to engage.
The future is not denied by ⁧لَا⁩ . Use ⁧لَنْ⁩ + conjunctive , without ⁧سَـ⁩ and without ⁧سَوْفَ⁩ :
⁧سَيَأْتُونَ.⁩ ⁧لَنْ يَأْتُوا.⁩ They're not coming.

⁧لَنْ⁩ It's a strong negation: "I won't... (and I won't) " Many Arabic speakers deny the future with dialectal forms in their daily speech; in the written and formal standard the correct form is always ⁧لَنْ⁩ .
The conjunctive is obtained from the indicative imperfection with two changes, which you have already seen announced in A2-03 (section 2):
1. the final -u becomes -a: ⁧يَدْرُسُ⁩ → ⁧يَدْرُسَ⁩ ;
2. terminations -īna, -āni, -ūna I forgive the -na / -ni: ⁧تَدْرُسِينَ⁩ → ⁧تَدْرُسِي⁩ , ⁧يَدْرُسَانِ⁩ → ⁧يَدْرُسَا⁩ , ⁧يَدْرُسُونَ⁩ → ⁧يَدْرُسُوا⁩
(with the breathless, like the perfect). The -na of the female plural ( ⁧تَدْرُسْنَ⁩ , ⁧يَدْرُسْنَ⁩ ) does not fall: it is not a termination of the indication.

blocks.text: Culture. Refusal of an invitation with a dry "no" sounds rude almost everywhere in the Arab world. You always thank yourself, give yourself a reason and leave an open door. On the contrary, if God wants it without further details, it can be a kind rejection: if you need a precise answer, ask for a date.
